## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If AGENTS.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session (its first 64 KiB); your other files are there to read with the file tools. What a later session knows of your earlier games is what you have left in these files.

## This game

A new game. You play White, so your opponent moves first, right after you choose it.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: `read_file(path)` and `list_files(path)` to read, and `apply_patch` to create, change and delete any file in your working directory.

You may write and run code. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.
I’ll stay at 20k for game 26, read the latest review, and record every position. I’ll focus on developing enough area early and securing eye boundaries before a group gets enclosed.

# Game 25: Black vs 20k — W+4

Played 2026-10-06. 9×9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Consecutive passes at moves52–53 ended the game.
Black42, White39+7=46. Captures: Black1, White7.
The 20k record is four wins, sixteen losses and one draw. Retain20k.

## Records and verification

- game-025.sgf records all53 moves:50 stone moves and three passes.
- game-025-log.json contains opponent selection, all27 play responses including the final score, every returned board, group/liberty and empty-region inventories, decision notes, exact moves, capture events and final counts.
- The first returned playing-board inventory was reconstructed afterward; subsequent playing inventories were computed during play.
- Replay of the actual recorded moves reproduced every returned board and capture count.
- The official W+4 agrees with independent42–39 area counting. No dead stones remained to remove during scoring.
- No invalid move, attempted ko recapture or resignation occurred.
- Code only inspected returned boards, kept records, converted actual moves to SGF, counted area and replayed historical moves. All move choices and hypothetical lines were manual. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search or automated move selection/ranking/recommendation.

## Opening and the insufficient lower outline

1 B C3, 2 W F7, 3 B G3, 4 W C6,
5 B E4, 6 W E5, 7 B F5, 8 W D5,
9 B F4, 10 W F6, 11 B G6, 12 W G7,
13 B G5, 14 W H6, 15 B H5, 16 W J6.

C3/G3 developed both lower corners, but they were footholds in one lower region, not two independent territorial regions. F4 joined E4/F5. G6 initially had G5/H6 after G7; G5 promptly connected it through F5 before White H6. H5 prevented that contact stone from descending freely.

Before move9, a selected unsecured target was rows1–4=36, F/G/H/J row5=4, G/H/J rows6–7=6, total46. It needed numerous unplayed boundaries and supplied no eye proof.

The note before move13 revised that46 to43 because G7 was White. That subtraction was wrong: removing only G7 gives45 (36+4+3+2). After White H6, that same selected outline would be44, still counting unprotected J6/H7/J7. White J6 then occupied another target point. The later41 outline used a narrower selection: rows1–4=36, F/G/H/J row5=4, G6=1. This was a new conditional outline, not a justified automatic ownership forecast.

The deficit was recognized around moves13–16, but the next moves remained lower boundary repairs. Earlier second-base development or different middle-boundary choices remain hypotheses, not verified winning replacements. The outcome does not establish C3, G3, E4 or the hane itself as intrinsically wrong.

## C4 capture and prompt connection

17 B D4, 18 W C4, 19 B B4, 20 W B5,
21 B C5 captured C4, 22 W A5, 23 B C4, 24 W B7.

D4 held the lower central boundary. White C4 was disconnected with B4/C5; Black B4 left it only C5. White B5 ignored this atari. Black C5 captured C4, opening C4 for neighboring B4, C3 and D4 groups.

The capturing C5 stone itself had only C4. Immediate White C4 would have captured C5 and exactly restored the preceding board, so simple ko would prohibit it. This transient ko is manually inferred; the returned board came after White A5 and showed ko none. No recapture was attempted.

Black C4 immediately joined C5/B4/C3/D4. Do not count the capture as secured without that connection. The lower conditional outline then became42:
rows1–4 all36, C5/F5/G5/H5/J5 five, G6 one.
This depended on retaining the open bottom and lower edge boundaries; the eventual game did retain all42.

The gain relied on the actual ignored atari, not a forced capture against every White response. Before the capture, any full rows1–4 target including White C4 needed to label it as an enemy recovery target.

## Top-center development: connections without eyes

25 B D7, 26 W D6, 27 B C7, 28 W B8,
29 B E7, 30 W B6, 31 B C8, 32 W E8,
33 B D8, 34 W F8, 35 B D9, 36 W E9.

D7 sought extra area while C/D/E rows7–9 were still open. The named nine-point target was only potential. It required left/right endpoint boundaries and dividing moves that were not secured.

White D6 joined C6/D5/E5 and denied a direct lower connection. C7 joined D7 and cut the B7/C6 route, but B6 simply joined White's left and central stones later. E7 extended the upper group; C8 protected the left endpoint from B8. Neither move established eyes.

White E8 occupied the internal/right boundary before Black could secure it. D8 joined the upper stones, but White F8 connected E8 to the right White chain. D9 connected safely; White E9 then denied the top-right endpoint.

After move36, six Black stones C7/C8/D7/D8/D9/E7 had exactly C9/E6. C9 was not a true eye because B9 was empty; E6 was an outside liberty bordered by White D6/E5/F6. No two-eye or escape proof existed.

A note before move25 named C9/E9 as prospective eyes and listed several required boundaries. That was insufficient planning: both depended on contested corner/first-line endpoints, and White E8/E9 took the right boundary before the necessary turns. Named eyes and broad geometric room do not prove that a base can obtain them in time.

Earlier top endpoint choices or earlier D7 development are unverified candidates. The manual analysis did not exhaust every remote rescue. The exact played closure and limited failed extensions are sufficient evidence for the failure, without claiming a universal proof at move36.

37 B J5, 38 W H8, 39 B A4, 40 W E6,
41 B J7, 42 W H7, 43 B F3, 44 W J8,
45 B H4, 46 W C9 captured all six upper stones.

White E6 at40 joined the White chains and left the upper group only C9. At that position:
B C9 adds B9 and leaves seven stones only B9;
W B9 joins B8 and captures seven immediately.
There is no further Black turn to play A9 after that capture.
Actual Black stopped adding stones, and White C9 captured the six at46.

An in-analysis branch briefly treated A8 as already White; the returned board shows A8 EMPTY. That assumption was discarded. Do not transfer the hypothetical branch into a death proof. The exact E6/C9/B9 line above uses the actual board.

## Reject the immediate capture; distinguish the two-liberty atari

Before move39, Black H7 was considered and rejected:
G7/H6/H8 were White, J7 empty, so the new H7 stone would have only J7.
It would atari H6/J6 at J7, but White J7 would join those stones and capture H7 immediately, reopening H7. This is the same failure mechanism as earlier one-liberty threats.

Actual Black J7 at41 was different. Its two liberties were H7/J8, and it ataried H6/J6 at H7. White could not capture J7 in one immediate move. If White ignored the atari, Black H7 would capture two, opening H6/J6; a prompt connection through H6 or J6 would then be available. This was a conditional tactical opportunity, not a forcing territorial gain.

White H7 correctly answered by connecting H6/J6 to G7/H8 and the large White group. J7 then had only J8:
B J8 would leave two stones only J9;
W J9 captures both, opening J8 for the new White stone.
An in-game note incorrectly said this extension would capture THREE. The actual line captures TWO; J7/J8 are the only Black stones in it.
Black abandoned J7, and White J8 captured that one stone at44. Do not extend this strip after H7 closes its base.

## Lower life and exact final score

F3 at43 joined G3 through F4. H4 at45 joined H5 and secured true G4:
F4/G3/G5/H4 all belonged to one connected Black group.

47 B D3, 48 W C8, 49 B F2, 50 W pass,
51 B E2, 52 W pass, 53 B pass.

D3 joined C3/D4. F2 joined F3, allowing E2 to join through F2. E3 then had connected Black boundaries D3/E2/E4/F3. E2 alone would have been disconnected before F2; that extra connection was explicitly accounted for.

E3 and G4 are independent true eyes. At either White fill, Black retains the other eye, so nothing is captured and the move is suicide. All nineteen surviving Black stones live in one group.

Black19 stones+23 territory=42.
Territory: A1/A2/A3/B1/B2/B3/C1/C2/D1/D2/E1/F1/G1/G2/H1/H2/H3/J1/J2/J3/J4, E3, G4.
Rows1–9:9,9,9,9,5,1,0,0,0.

White23 stones+16 territory=39.
Empty regions: A6/A7/A8/A9/B9 (five);
C7/D7/D8/D9/E7 (five);
J7 (one);
F9/G8/G9/H9/J9 (five).
Each region has only connected White boundaries. Multiple separated eye regions establish White life.
Rows1–9:0,0,0,0,4,8,9,9,9.

No neutral points. White39+7=46 versus Black42: W+4.
Two points shifted from White to Black would draw at44–37; three would win at45–36. No specific three-point winning replacement is verified.

## Carry forward

1. Retain20k: four wins, sixteen losses, one draw.
2. Count early, then act while a second base can obtain its boundaries. The 41/42 lower deficit was identified before the top entry, but six top moves built a connected strip without eyes.
3. Reconsider the upper plan before E8/F8/E9 closes it. C8/D8/D9 connections did not provide a second eye; E6 was not one.
4. Keep the precise C5/C4 capture-and-connection habit, while recognizing that White B5 ignored the atari and the isolated capturer initially had a transient ko vulnerability.
5. Reject H7's immediate-capture threat. J7 had two liberties and a conditional capture benefit, but White H7 answered it; stop extending after that connection.
6. Preserve the supported lower E3/G4 life proof and42 count. They survived without a lower capture or rescue, but that framework still lacked three shifted points for a win.
7. Correct arithmetic and extension counts explicitly:46 minus G7 is45; J7/J8 comprises TWO stones. Read actual board neighbors, including empty A8.

Script completed

const review=`# Game 26: White vs 20k — B+30

Played 2026-10-06. 9×9, Chinese area scoring, komi7, simple ko.

The 20k record is four wins, seventeen losses and one draw. Retain20k.

## Records and verification

- game-026-log.json saves opponent selection and all32 play responses, every returned position, move choices and notes, group/liberty and empty-region inventories, exact moves and corrected final counts.

## Opening: early opposite foothold did not establish enough area

1 B E5, 2 W C3, 3 B D3, 4 W C4,
5 B C5, 6 W G7, 7 B D4, 8 W C2,
9 B D2, 10 W B4, 11 B B5, 12 W C1,
13 B F7, 14 W F8, 15 B E6, 16 W G8,
17 B E8, 18 W C7, 19 B D7, 20 W C6,
21 B C8, 22 W B7, 23 B D6.

G7 supplied an opposite-side foothold early, but the lower-left C-line was pressed against the edge. C1 secured a first-line boundary; it did not supply two eyes. B4 prevented an immediate B4 undercut but Black B5 still limited the base.

F8 hane had E8/F9/G8 liberties; G8 promptly joined F8 to G7. Black E8 then divided the broad upper target. White C7 sought an upper-left region while room remained, but C6 prioritized downward expansion and Black C8 denied the top route. B7 preserved left access; Black D6 connected D7 to E6/E5 and closed central escape.

An early broad geometric target was lower A-C rows1–4=12 plus upper rows6–9=36, total48. This was merely selected room, not secure ownership. Before G8 a narrower target was lower12 plus rows8–9=18 plus A-E row7=5 plus G/H/J rows6–7=6, total41; most boundaries were unplayed and the region was still globally connected through open points. Black E8 occupied one target point and split access.

After C8/D6, upper-left A/B rows6–9 plus C6/C7 would be10; lower12 plus a roughly18-point upper-right target would total40 only if all three bases survived. No two-eye proof supported that total. The opponent directly occupied their required endpoints.

C8 instead of C6 at20, B6 before B9, or a different earlier side/boundary strategy remain hypotheses. No single saving or winning replacement is verified.

## Upper-left: protect both endpoints before making edge stones

24 W B8, 25 B C9, 26 W B9, 27 B B6,
28 W A7, 29 B A6.

B8/B9 secured the upper corner boundary but allowed Black B6 to deny the lower boundary. After27, five White stones B7/B8/B9/C6/C7 had exactly A7/A8/A9. This was an edge strip with unsecured A6, not two eyes.

A7 added one real outside liberty A6, but Black immediately occupied it and joined A6 to B6/B5/C5. Six White stones A7/B7/B8/B9/C6/C7 then had only A8/A9, one two-point eye space.

A local exact final-position capture line is:
B A8, W A9 joins B9 and captures the invading A8 stone,
B A8 captures all seven White stones.
The second Black A8 joins A7's enemy boundary through A6 and consumes the joined group's last liberty. This is not a ko capture: seven stones are removed. Alternatively B A9 leaves the six White stones only A8; W A8 is suicide because Black A9 retains A8, and B A8 captures six.

White stopped adding stones. No exhaustive remote rescue was searched. The played closure and direct edge capture are sufficient evidence for the final dead-group exclusion.

## Lower-left: safe atari, answered connection, and corrected four-point trap

30 W G6, 31 B G5, 32 W H5, 33 B A2,
34 W B2, 35 B A3, 36 W A4, 37 B D1,
38 W A5, 39 B D5.

G6/H5 began right-side expansion. H5 had H4/H6/J5, so it was not an immediately capturable one-liberty threat.

B2 confined the lower invasion but did not secure eyes. A4 joined B4 and blocked A3's upward route. Black D1 closed the last bottom exit. A5 now safely joined A4 and ataried A6/B5/B6/C5 at D5. Black D5 answered by joining those stones to the entire central and D-line group.

Earlier A5, before White A4, would instead have had only A4. Black A4 could capture it immediately, opening A5 for B5/A6. The same coordinate became a safe atari only after its supporting connection existed. The actual atari was answered, not ignored; no rescue occurred.

After39, eight lower White stones A4/A5/B2/B4/C1/C2/C3/C4 had only B1/B3. Black A2/A3 had A1/B3. Black could fill B1, leaving White only B3; W B3 would consume its last liberty without capturing because Black A2/A3 retained A1, so it would be suicide. Black could then capture at B3.

Black's actual A1 at57 joined A2/A3. Both opposing groups then had B1/B3. Post-game I briefly suspected seki because a Black initiation followed by White's capture would open four points. That claim was wrong and explicitly discarded: the four-point shape and the divider's actual connections matter.

Exact final-board local kill:
B B1 joins A1/A2/A3, leaving the eight-stone White group only B3.
W B3 captures Black A1/A2/A3/B1 and joins B2/B4/C3.
The nine-stone White group now borders empty A1/A2/A3/B1.
B A2 takes the dividing point, with A1/A3 liberties.

Responses:
- W A3 joins A4/B3 but leaves the ten-stone group only B1; B B1 captures ten.
- W B1 joins B2/C1 but leaves the ten-stone group only A3; B A3 joins A2 and captures ten.
- W A1 is ISOLATED: B1 is empty, A2 is Black. It has only B1. B B1 captures that one stone and leaves the nine-stone main group only A3. W A3 is suicide because Black A2 retains the reopened A1; Black A3 captures nine.
- Playing elsewhere allows Black A3 to atari the main group at B1, then capture there. White B1 would be suicide because the Black A2/A3 group retains A1.

The W A1 branch creates an inferred transient ko at A1 after B B1 captures one isolated stone with only A1 as its liberty. Immediate W A1 would restore the preceding board and is forbidden. A remote ko threat does not force a response: Black can capture the nine-stone main group at A3. No such branch or ko was actually played.

Do not assume every Black initiation is equivalent: B B3 first opens a different four-point shape after W B1. The verified killing initiation is B1, followed by A2. Two opposing-color shared liberties and four opened points do not establish seki. My proposed A1 divider failed the same orthogonal-connection test that earlier sessions repeatedly missed.

## Right: supported connections and explicit life

40 W G4, 41 B F5, 42 W F4, 43 B F6,
44 W E4, 45 B E3, 46 W F3, 47 B F2,
48 W H4, 49 B G2, 50 W H6, 51 B H3,
52 W H8, 53 B F9, 54 W G9, 55 B E9,
56 W J8, 57 B A1, 58 W J6, 59 B J3,
60 W G3, 61 B H2, 62 W J4, 63 B E7,

G4 had F4/G3/H4 and ataried G5 at F5. Black F5 connected G5 to the central group. F4/E4/F3 made connected downward extensions, but E3/F2/G2 steadily removed the bottom outline. H4 joined G4/F4/F3/E4 to H5 before their liberties narrowed further. H6 then joined this lower chain to G6/G7/G8/F8.

At move50 the selected conditional right outline was29:
rows1/2 H/J=4;
row3 F/G/H/J=4;
row4 E/F/G/H/J=5;
row5 H/J=2;
rows6/7 G/H/J=6;
rows8/9 F/G/H/J=8.
It was already short of38, and Black H3/J3/H2/F9/E9 removed seven further target points. Recognition came too late to obtain another viable base.

H8 joined G8 and secured the corner boundary. G9 blocked Black F9's extension; E9 connected F9 to E8. J8 joined H8 and secured independent true two-point H9/J9, bounded by G9/H8/J8. J6 joined H6 and secured true two-point H7/J7, bounded by G7/H6/H8/J6/J8. All boundaries belong to one White group, so an attempted opponent fill retains another eye and captures nothing; the spaces cannot both be destroyed.

G3 added no liberties: F3/G4 were White, G2/H3 Black. It was safe because life was already proved, and secured its area point. J4 joined H4 and supplied a third true eye J5 with H5/J4/J6 boundaries. None of H7/J7 or H9/J9 was filled to make an unnecessary connection.

This seventeen-stone right group survived without captures. It established life, not enough area.

## Final count

Manually remove the six upper-left and eight lower-left dead White stones. The engine's final display retained all fourteen, and captures remained0 each.

White17 stones+5 territory=22.
True empty regions: H7/J7 (2), H9/J9 (2), J5 (1).
Rows1–9 White:0,0,2,5,2,3,3,4,3.

Black32 stones+27 territory=59.
Empty regions after dead-stone exclusion:
A7/A8/A9/B7/B8/B9/C6/C7 (8);
D8/D9 (2);
A4/A5/B1/B2/B3/B4/C1/C2/C3/C4 (10);
E1/E2/F1/G1/H1/J1/J2 (7).
Rows1–9 Black:9,9,7,4,7,6,6,5,6.
No neutral area. Black59 versus White22+7=29: B+30.

The post-game seki suspicion would have invalidated this count if correct; the exact B1/A2 kill corrected it. The final independent count therefore matches the official result. Historical replay verifies actual boards and captures, not hypothetical variations.

## Carry forward

1. Retain20k: four wins, seventeen losses, one draw.
2. Early opposite footholds are not enough. Upper-left B8/B9 secured one endpoint while B6/A6 closed the other; prioritize the whole eye boundary and playable route before stacking edge stones.
3. Count prospective area early, then revise when an enemy occupies a needed boundary. Forty conditional points across three unsettled bases is not a dependable winning framework.
4. Keep prompt real connections F8–G8, G4–F4, H4–H5, H6–G6, G9–G8, J8–H8 and J6–H6. The right group secured three independent eye spaces without a capture.
5. A supported threat can still be answered. A5 became safe only after A4; D5 simply connected Black. G4's safe atari likewise received F5. Do not rely on ignored ataris.
6. Rebuild a proposed divider's actual orthogonal neighbors. In the lower four-point shape, A1 was isolated, even though the rest of the boundary was connected White. The transient ko after its capture did not protect the main group's last liberty.
7. Preserve exact corrected life/death proofs, not the initial seki guess. Opening alternatives remain hypotheses; no move is established as optimal by this loss.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. The final seven-stone White right group had only H4 and J2 as liberties and a concrete forced-capture route. Connected second-line stones do not guarantee a base.
8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.
11. Three connected empty edge points are not already two eyes. In game 3, White J8 occupied the middle of J7/J8/J9. Black J7, White J5 left the seven-stone upper-right group with only J9. Black J9 would capture J8 but leave the entire eight-stone group with only J8; White J8 captures it all. This is not ko. Simply substituting J8 for J6 at move 61 was not verified to save it: J6 also needed boundary protection.
12. Check the hane's cut and the new stone's own liberties. Game 3's A5 was left in atari by White B5; A6 was suicide. White A6 later captured A5 and reopened A5 for the neighboring White edge group. Black A1 then had only B1, and White B1 captured it, reopening A1. Both planned edge squeezes ignored liberties opened by captures.
13. An invasion can gain connected stones without gaining a base. Game 3's C8/D8/D7/C7/B7/D9 ended with only B8 and C9 as liberties. White A8/A7 and E9 denied eye boundaries. The later upper-right entry also failed; neither upper group was saved.
14. An extension must actually reach open space. In game 4, F4/F5/F6/E6 grew a connected chain without eyes. After Black E7, its remaining liberties were G1, G5, J1, J2, J3; the central escape was closed. The inventory ran every move, but did not prevent this strategic failure. Re-evaluate before the final route narrows to one point.
15. Preserving one corner boundary does not establish two eyes. Game 4's H1 prevented game 2's undercut, but Black H4 restricted the upper base. J3/J4/J5 added occupied edge stones, not eyes. At the end the thirteen-stone White group had only J1/J2: one two-point eye space. Black J2, White J1 captures one stone, Black J2 captures fourteen; this is not ko.
16. A threat may be answered by capturing its new stone. Game 4's G7 threatened Black G5/G6/H4/H5 but had only G8. Black G8 captured it and reopened G7 for three adjacent Black groups. Do not count such a threat as forcing.
17. Count playable escape points, not just raw liberties. In game 5, the top D8/D9/E8/E9 block had only D7, but Black D7 was suicide: White C7, D6 and E7 surrounded it and none would be captured. After White C8 at move 32, D9/E9 added stones without creating eyes or escape. The E8/F8/D8/C8/D9/C9/E9/F9 continuation failed.
18. A surviving framework can still be too small. Game 5's lower group scored 38 area against White's 43 plus komi. At that split, shifting six points from White to Black only draws; seven wins. Contest additional space before D6/F6 and the upper boundary close, rather than relying on a late first-line invasion.
19. Two shared liberties do not prove seki. In game 6 after move 19, White's eight-stone lower-left group and Black A2/B2 both had only A1/A3. Black A3, White A1 captured three, but Black A2 then occupied the vital point of A2/A3/B2. White A3 allows Black B2 to capture ten; White B2 allows Black A3 to capture ten. White instead played elsewhere and Black A3/B2 captured nine. The earlier claim of seki was wrong. Read beyond the first capture to the opponent's next turn.
20. A capture into a three-point eye space needs the dividing point before it supplies two eyes. In game 6, White A2 after capturing A2/A3/B2 would divide A3 and B2, but Black moved first and killed. By contrast, the upper group already had true eyes B9 (A9/B8/C9 boundaries) and E9 (D9/E8/F9 boundaries) before capturing H8/H9; all boundaries were connected White.
21. Reassess a second eye's boundary immediately after an undercut. Game 6 preserved J1 with H1/J2, but G1 required a surviving White F1 boundary. Black F2/F1/E1 connected to D1–D4, so G1 was not an eye. E4/F4/G4 led into a closed strip; Black G1/E4/F4/G4 left the eight-stone White group only J1, and Black J1 captured it. H1 alone again did not establish life.

White H9 could capture two and open F9/G9 for the invaders. Actual White J9 at move 52 captured F9/G9/H9 and reopened F9/G9/H9. Black's attempted chase did not force a capture.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. The final seven-stone White right group had only H4 and J2 as liberties and a concrete forced-capture route. Connected second-line stones do not guarantee a base.
8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.
11. Three connected empty edge points are not already two eyes. In game 3, White J8 occupied the middle of J7/J8/J9. Black J7, White J5 left the seven-stone upper-right group with only J9. Black J9 would capture J8 but leave the entire eight-stone group with only J8; White J8 captures it all. This is not ko. Simply substituting J8 for J6 at move 61 was not verified to save it: J6 also needed boundary protection.
12. Check the hane's cut and the new stone's own liberties. Game 3's A5 was left in atari by White B5; A6 was suicide. White A6 later captured A5 and reopened A5 for the neighboring White edge group. Black A1 then had only B1, and White B1 captured it, reopening A1. Both planned edge squeezes ignored liberties opened by captures.
13. An invasion can gain connected stones without gaining a base. Game 3's C8/D8/D7/C7/B7/D9 ended with only B8 and C9 as liberties. White A8/A7 and E9 denied eye boundaries. The later upper-right entry also failed; neither upper group was saved.
14. An extension must actually reach open space. In game 4, F4/F5/F6/E6 grew a connected chain without eyes. After Black E7, its remaining liberties were G1, G5, J1, J2, J3; the central escape was closed. The inventory ran every move, but did not prevent this strategic failure. Re-evaluate before the final route narrows to one point.
15. Preserving one corner boundary does not establish two eyes. Game 4's H1 prevented game 2's undercut, but Black H4 restricted the upper base. J3/J4/J5 added occupied edge stones, not eyes. At the end the thirteen-stone White group had only J1/J2: one two-point eye space. Black J2, White J1 captures one stone, Black J2 captures fourteen; this is not ko.
16. A threat may be answered by capturing its new stone. Game 4's G7 threatened Black G5/G6/H4/H5 but had only G8. Black G8 captured it and reopened G7 for three adjacent Black groups. Do not count such a threat as forcing.
17. Count playable escape points, not just raw liberties. In game 5, the top D8/D9/E8/E9 block had only D7, but Black D7 was suicide: White C7, D6 and E7 surrounded it and none would be captured. After White C8 at move 32, D9/E9 added stones without creating eyes or escape. The E8/F8/D8/C8/D9/C9/E9/F9 continuation failed.
18. A surviving framework can still be too small. Game 5's lower group scored 38 area against White's 43 plus komi. At that split, shifting six points from White to Black only draws; seven wins. Contest additional space before D6/F6 and the upper boundary close, rather than relying on a late first-line invasion.
19. Two shared liberties do not prove seki. In game 6 after move 19, White's eight-stone lower-left group and Black A2/B2 both had only A1/A3. Black A3, White A1 captured three, but Black A2 then occupied the vital point of A2/A3/B2. White A3 allows Black B2 to capture ten; White B2 allows Black A3 to capture ten. White instead played elsewhere and Black A3/B2 captured nine. The earlier claim of seki was wrong. Read beyond the first capture to the opponent's next turn.
20. A capture into a three-point eye space needs the dividing point before it supplies two eyes. In game 6, White A2 after capturing A2/A3/B2 would divide A3 and B2, but Black moved first and killed. By contrast, the upper group already had true eyes B9 (A9/B8/C9 boundaries) and E9 (D9/E8/F9 boundaries) before capturing H8/H9; all boundaries were connected White.
21. Reassess a second eye's boundary immediately after an undercut. Game 6 preserved J1 with H1/J2, but G1 required a surviving White F1 boundary. Black F2/F1/E1 connected to D1–D4, so G1 was not an eye. E4/F4/G4 led into a closed strip; Black G1/E4/F4/G4 left the eight-stone White group only J1, and Black J1 captured it. H1 alone again did not establish life.
